title: Change Blindness
scopeNote: This keeps the flicker paradigm and the with-blank against no-blank comparison, which is the whole argument. The bank of scenes, the controls over what changes and where, and the comparison table across every run stay in the longer version, and the page says so. One design change was made rather than inherited: the two runs use different scenes, because running the same scene twice means the second search is faster partly because the learner already knows the answer.
summary: A street scene alternates with itself, with a blank quarter-second in between, and one large thing keeps changing. Most people cannot find it. The same task with the blank removed, on a fresh scene, takes a moment.
learningObjectives: Explain what the blank interval does to the local signal a change normally produces.
Predict and then check how much easier the same kind of change becomes without a blank.
Explain why change blindness does not show that people store nothing about a scene.
Recognise that a slow search is time spent attending elsewhere rather than time spent blind.
Say why comparing two runs of the same scene would not be a fair comparison.
interactionTypes: a performed flicker search with the learner's own search time recorded
an identification step that verifies the change was actually found
a reveal that rings the changed object on the picture
a second run on a fresh scene with the blank removed
a manual stepping route that never moves on its own
privacy: Nothing is collected, stored or transmitted. Search times are measured in the browser and are gone when the page is closed.
accessibilityNotes: The picture alternates about 1.2 times a second, well below the 3 Hz associated with photosensitive seizures, nothing is bright or high contrast, and the page says so before anything starts. A manual stepping route is offered to everyone from the start rather than hidden behind a media query: it moves only when a button is pressed and is the route for anyone who has asked for reduced motion. Nothing is ever timed out and a way to end the search is available throughout. The scene carries a description naming what it contains and which version is showing, and at the reveal it states in words what changed, so the demonstration does not depend on seeing the picture. The identification options are named parts of the scene, keyboard operable, and marked with a glyph and a hidden note as well as a colour. Every stage is announced through a polite live region.
dataStatus: Two invented scenes, drawn from simple shapes. The search times are the learner's own. Nothing is a norm.
simulationNotes: 600 ms per picture and 250 ms of blank, as in the original. The two runs deliberately use different scenes. The original runs the same scene both ways and notes in its own documentation that this is the one comparison its design supports; that works as a classroom demonstration because most people fail with the blank, but anyone who does find the change then searches the second run already knowing the answer. Using a second scene costs nothing pedagogically and makes the comparison honest, and the caution states what was done and why. Pressing the found button stops the clock, and the learner must then say which object changed: without that step the recorded time would measure confidence rather than detection.
readmeTopic: why a quarter-second of blank makes a large obvious change nearly impossible to find
